Eighth grade science · Unit 8.2

Energy Transformation & Conservation

Unit 2: Thermal Energy and Unit 3: Forces, Motion and Energy introduced energy; Unit 7.3 followed it through chemical reactions. Now we put numbers on it. Energy is never created or destroyed, only moved and changed. Use the claim-evidence-reasoning habit from Unit 0: How Science Works when your numbers do not seem to add up.

Where we left off: Unit 8.1 covered forces and momentum in collisions. You may already have learned that energy changes form (Units 2, 3, and 7.3). Now we track the amounts: kinetic and potential energy, waste heat, and efficiency.

Concept 1 · Energy transformations

Energy changes form, never disappears

Energy shows up as motion (kinetic), position (potential), thermal, chemical, electrical, light, and sound. Devices transform one form into others.

Analogy

Money in different pockets

Ten dollars can be cash, a gift card, or a bank balance. It is the same ten dollars in different forms; energy works the same way.

Concept 2 · Roller coaster

Trading height for speed

Gravitational potential energy grows with height and mass; kinetic energy = ½ × mass × speed². On a frictionless track their sum stays the same, so they trade.

Analogy

Savings and spending

At the top of a hill you have lots saved (potential). Rolling down, you spend it as speed (kinetic). At the bottom you have spent it all, but no money vanished.

Try it

Ride the coaster

Data

Speed at the bottom

Drop heightSpeed at bottom (no friction)
5 m10 m/s (36 km/h)
20 m20 m/s (72 km/h)
45 m30 m/s (108 km/h)
80 m40 m/s (144 km/h)

Speed = √(2 g h), so doubling speed needs four times the height.

Concept 3 · Why speed matters most

Doubling speed quadruples kinetic energy

Kinetic energy depends on speed squared. That is why highway crashes are far worse than parking-lot bumps, and why speed limits matter.

Analogy

Doubling speed, quadruple energy

Running at twice the speed does not cost double the energy: it costs four times as much, because kinetic energy depends on speed squared. Each extra bit of speed gets expensive. Where it breaks: this is the energy of motion only; a real runner also spends energy on muscles, heat, and air resistance.

Concept 4 · Conservation and waste heat

Where does the energy go?

Total energy is conserved, but some always turns into thermal energy by friction and drag, spreading out where we cannot use it. Efficiency = useful energy out ÷ total energy in.

Analogy

A leaky bucket

Pour 10 liters in and only 6 reach the end: 4 leaked out. The water was not destroyed, but it was not useful there. Waste heat is the leak.

Try it

Bouncing ball

Data

Efficiency

Concept 5 · Using energy wisely

Efficient design saves money and resources

Engineers raise efficiency by cutting friction, adding insulation, or choosing better devices. Savings are measured in energy and dollars.

Analogy

Plug the leaks

An old house loses heat like a bucket full of holes. Insulation plugs them.

Check yourself

Can you explain it?

A ball dropped from 2 m only bounces back to 1.4 m. Where did the missing energy go, and how does that fit the law of conservation of energy?

Show a model answer

Some energy turned into thermal energy and sound when the ball hit the floor (the ball and floor warmed slightly) and into internal deformation. The total energy is the same, but less of it is kinetic/potential in the ball, so the bounce is lower.

0 of 6 correct

Words to know

kinetic energy
Energy of motion.
potential energy
Stored energy because of position.
conservation of energy
Energy cannot be created or destroyed.
transformation
Change from one form to another.
efficiency
Useful energy out divided by energy in.
joule
Unit of energy.
watt
Joules per second; unit of power.
thermal energy
Energy of particle motion.
friction
Force that turns motion into heat.
system
The objects you decide to track.
Tutor notes: hands-on kit, misconceptions, pacing

Kit (about $8): a ramp and a marble/toy car, a meter stick, bouncy balls, a stopwatch, a thermometer, a kilowatt meter ($20, optional), LED and incandescent bulbs.

  • Concept 1: Roll a marble from different heights and measure speed (distance/time).
  • Concept 2: Drop balls from 1 m and record bounce heights, graph results.
  • Concept 3: Rub hands and feel the heat: motion to thermal.
  • Concept 4: Measure phone-charger watts with a meter if available.
  • Concept 5: Do a home energy hunt: list five devices and their energy forms.

Common misconceptions:

  • "Energy gets used up." It changes form.
  • "Potential energy only exists on high things." Springs, batteries and food hold it too.
  • "Heavier objects fall faster." Heavier means more energy, not more speed.
  • "Efficiency of 100% is possible." Some heat always escapes.

Pacing: about five 30-minute sessions. Method link: ask students to define the system, write the prediction, and use a data table with several trials (Unit 0).

After the lesson · Game

Play: Energy Chain

Build a three-stage energy chain from a 1,000 J source. Each device has an efficiency, so every stage shrinks the useful energy and adds waste heat. Match the energy forms and hit the target.
